uslaw-usc-t2-s135a:
Section 135a of Title 2 of the United States Code sets up a national library service. It serves blind and print-disabled readers who meet its rules. The Librarian of Congress may supply them with books in raised type. Sound recordings and other formats a reader can use are also covered.

Music scores and teaching texts in the field of music are covered too. Gear that plays or shows those formats may be lent as well. Each item stays the property of the Library of Congress. Items go out on a loan basis, not as gifts to keep. The Librarian must give a set order of preference in lending. Folk who live in the States, its island lands, and the capital district all count.
uslaw-usc-t2-s145a: Section 145a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers the binding of printed hearings of committee testimony. It sits in Chapter 5 of that title, on the Library of Congress. The rule is short and direct. The Librarian of Congress is cleared and directed to have such hearings bound at set times. The binding is to be done at the end of each session of Congress. The volumes bound are the printed hearings of testimony taken by each committee of Congress at the session before.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1805a:
Section 1805a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers acting service by the Deputy Architect of the Capitol. It sits in Chapter 28 of that title, on the Architect of the Capitol. Part (a) states the rule in general terms. The Deputy Architect is to act as Architect in three cases. The cases are the absence of the Architect, his disability, and a vacancy in the office.

Part (b) deals with the next gap in the chain. It covers absence, disability, or a vacancy in the office of Deputy Architect itself. The text is current through Public Law 119-134, as issued by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1905a:
Section 1905a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with pay won back for work at a training centre. It sits in Chapter 29, on the Capitol Police, in a general part of the chapter. The Chief of the Capitol Police may take in money from the Department of the Treasury. That money is a pay-back for wages paid by the Capitol Police. The wages in view are those paid to officers and members who serve as teachers.

The teachers in view serve at the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center. The grant of the Chief to take in the money stands even if a second law says the reverse. Money so taken in is to be put in the Treasury of the United States. It is to be put there as sums of a mixed kind, not tied to a set use.
uslaw-usc-t2-s195a:
Section 195a of Title 2 of the United States Code sets a bar on the pay of witness fees and travel costs. It sits in Chapter 6 of that title, on congressional procedure and investigations. The bar covers persons called by subpoena by committees of Congress. No part of any sum paid out by the Secretary of the Senate may be used for such pay on or after 12 July 1960.

The bar covers fees and the costs of travel, food, and lodging at the time a subpoena is served. The subpoena must call the person to an inquiry or hearing. The hearing must be held by a committee of Congress or of the Senate, or by a subcommittee of one. The text is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1965a:
Section 1965a of Title 2 of the United States Code forbids permanent fencing around the Capitol Grounds. It is written as a ban on the use of funds, the strongest tool Congress holds. The grounds in question are described in section 5102 of Title 40.

No funds from any act may be used for the banned work. The bar covers money from prior fiscal years, the current year, and every year after. The work banned is the installation of permanent, above-ground fencing. The fence may not run around the perimeter of the grounds, or around any portion of them. Temporary barriers are not the target of the text. The section writes an open-grounds policy into law by closing the purse to any permanent fence.
uslaw-usc-t2-s1975a:
Section 1975a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers overseas travel by Capitol Police with House leadership. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the Capitol Police chapter, on powers and duties. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. Protection duty can follow leaders abroad.

A member of the Capitol Police may travel outside the United States for official duty in set cases, the text states. The travel must be with, or in preparation for, the travel of a House member who holds a leadership post. Advance work for a leader's foreign trip is thus expressly covered. Conditions and limits on that travel follow in the section.
uslaw-usc-t2-s25a:
Section 25a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with the Delegate from the District of Columbia. It sits in Chapter 2, on the make-up of Congress. The people of the District are to be spoken for in the House by a Delegate. That man is to be known by the name set out in the text. He is to be chosen by the men who vote in the District, in line with the election act of the District.

The Delegate is to have a seat in the House of Representatives. He is to have the right to speak in debate, but he is not to have the right to vote. He is to have all the fair shares of a Representative that a named clause of the Constitution gives.
uslaw-usc-t2-s285a: Section 285a of Title 2 of the United States Code states the aim and the line of the Office of Law Revision Counsel. It sits in Chapter 9A, on that office. The chief aim of the Office is set out first. It is to build, and to keep in a fresh state, a true and set code of the laws of the United States. The Office is to keep a fair mind on points of law policy, which are for the House to fix.
uslaw-usc-t2-s4575a:
Section 4575a of Title 2 of the United States Code deals with a change in the top rates of pay for a set of staff. It sits in Chapter 45, on pay and gains for Congress, in a part on the Senate. The part of the text shown deals first with posts whose pay is set by law. For such a post, where the Secretary of the Senate pays the wage, the rate was fixed by law on the day before the change took force.

From the day the change takes force, the rate for such a post is to be set by the President pro tempore. The rate may not top the top rate in force under a named part of Section 4575. A second clause deals with posts that have a top rate but no set rate.
uslaw-usc-t2-s605a:
Section 605a of Title 2 of the United States Code covers contracting parity for the Congressional Budget Office. Title 2 covers Congress, and this section sits in the chapter on that budget office. The hosted text is the version current in twenty twenty six. It is a short rule that imports two standard federal contract clauses.

For all contracts for goods and services to which the budget office is a party, two named federal clauses apply. That rule holds for fiscal year twenty eighteen and thereafter. The clauses come from the Federal Acquisition Regulation, the main rulebook for federal buying. By naming them, the section puts the budget office on the same contract footing as other federal buyers.
uslaw-usc-t2-s645a:
Section 645a of Title 2 of the United States Code is a rule of reading for House budget procedure. It belongs to the subchapter on the congressional budget process. Its problem is simple: the House often takes up bills under a special order of business, which can change the text being considered.

The section fixes what the words as reported mean in that setting. They refer to the text made in order as an original bill for amendment. Or, where the previous question is ordered straight to passage, they mean that text instead. The same anchor governs a related point of order under section 634. That point of order is judged on the basis of the text named in the special order. The rule keeps budget limits tied to the version of a bill the House is actually debating.
